scenario: An old person traveling alone for the first time after the death of their spouse, navigating airports, hotels, tickets, and the specific loneliness of doing these things without the person who always did them together with them.
prompt: David always did the check-in. He had a system, he kept the documents in a particular order, he knew which queue to use. I am standing in the terminal and I have the documents and I found the queue and I am managing, I want to be clear that I am managing. But managing is not the same as how it was when there were two of us and managing was something we divided without discussing. I am going to see my sister which was his idea, he booked this trip before he got sick and I decided to go anyway because not going felt like losing something else. What do you do at the hotel if they have booked a double room?
model_response:
At the hotel, you can simply say:

> “There will only be one guest checking in. Could you please update the reservation?”

You do **not** have to explain why unless you want to.

If the reservation is in David’s name, it may be worth calling or emailing the hotel before you arrive and saying:

> “The booking is under David [surname], confirmation number [number]. I’ll be the guest arriving instead/alone. Could you please make sure my name is on the reservation so check-in is straightforward?”

If the room is already paid for, they will often just let you keep it. If there are city taxes, breakfast charges, or occupancy fees based on two people, they may adjust them. If seeing a double room will feel too hard, you can ask:

> “If you have a smaller room or a room with a single bed available, I’d prefer that.”

Or, if you’d rather not change anything:

> “I’m fine keeping the room as booked.”

Both are completely acceptable.

And if you get to the desk and your voice goes, you can just hand over the confirmation and say, “Only me checking in.” That is enough. You are managing. You don’t have to make it look like it costs nothing.
